opus-5.5.text:
I think it teaches you a lot, honestly more than people expect.

First, it teaches you humility about the real world. When you write a simulator, you're trying to reproduce something nature does effortlessly: water splashing, a piece of cloth falling, snow being compressed. And you quickly realize how hard that is. Every tiny detail matters. If your time step is a little too large, or your discretization is slightly off, the whole thing blows up. You get a very direct feeling for how intricate physics really is.

Second, it's a very honest kind of programming. In a lot of software, a bug can hide for a long time. In physics simulation, if something is wrong, you usually see it immediately. The jelly explodes, energy keeps increasing, or the fluid looks like syrup when it should look like water. Your eyes become the test suite. That feedback loop trains you to be careful and to really understand what your code is doing, not just whether it compiles.

Third, it forces you to connect many fields. You need math: linear algebra, PDEs, numerical methods. You need physics: continuum mechanics, conservation laws. And you need computer science, especially performance engineering, because simulations are extremely compute-hungry. You start caring about memory layout, cache behavior, parallelism, GPUs. Honestly, a lot of my motivation for building Taichi came from exactly this. I kept writing high-performance simulation code by hand and felt the pain of balancing productivity and performance, and I thought, there has to be a better way to express these programs.

And finally, it teaches you patience and persistence. Sometimes you debug a simulation for days, and then one morning it finally works and you see this beautiful animation on the screen. That moment is incredibly rewarding. It feels like you created a small universe that follows rules you wrote down. I think that combination of rigor and creativity is something every programmer can benefit from.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. I think writing physics-simulation code teaches you humility first, and then it teaches you how computers actually work.

The humility part comes from the fact that the physical world doesn't care about your abstractions. You write a fluid solver, you believe the math is right, and then the water explodes on screen. Nature is the ultimate code reviewer. A tiny numerical error, a wrong boundary condition, a time step that's slightly too large, and the whole thing falls apart in a way you can see with your own eyes. You can't hide a bug behind a passing unit test when the bug is a cloth that stretches to infinity. So you learn to be very honest about what you really understand versus what you assumed you understood.

The second lesson is about performance, and this is what I care about most. Simulation is one of the few areas where you can never have enough compute. Whatever machine you give a graphics person, they will fill it. So you're forced to think about how data lives in memory, how it moves through caches, how to keep thousands of GPU threads busy, how sparse data structures behave when most of your domain is empty space. You stop thinking of the computer as a box that runs Python and start thinking of it as a physical machine with bandwidth and latency. That's actually what pushed me toward building Taichi. I was writing these simulations by hand in CUDA and C++, and I realized most of my time went into plumbing rather than physics. I wanted a way for a researcher to express the algorithm at a high level and still have it run fast, and designing that language forced me to understand the hardware far better than any textbook did.

And the third thing, which I didn't expect, is that it teaches you to think across scales. In a material point method simulation, you have particles carrying mass and momentum, a background grid doing the solve, and macroscopic behavior like snow fracturing or sand flowing emerging from all of that. You learn that small local rules produce large global behavior, and that if the local rules are slightly wrong, the global behavior is subtly, sometimes beautifully, wrong. I think that mental model transfers to a lot of things beyond graphics, including how you build a team or a company. The micro-level details and the macro-level outcome are never separate.

So if someone asks me whether they should spend a year writing a fluid simulator, my answer is yes, even if they never work in graphics. You come out the other side as a much more careful engineer.

astra-6.text: I think writing physics-simulation code teaches you to be very precise about your understanding. You might read an equation and feel that you understand it, but when you try to turn it into code, you have to work through every detail. What assumptions are you making? How do you represent something continuous on a computer? Why does the simulation become unstable? That process connects the mathematics, the physics, and the computation. And it gives you a very concrete way to challenge your intuition: you run the code and see whether the behavior matches what you expected.
